extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government / political science and readers studying election law and party organization
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards about sources of party strength, abuses of party organization, and principles/features of election laws and ballot systems (vest-pocket vs. Australian ballots, ballot forms). A textbook-focused summary useful for analyzing or drafting election procedure reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public offices as a source of party funds
rubrics_metrics.description: There are...the public offices which are to be looked forward to as the legitimate reward of party services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that despite civil service reform, numerous federal, state, and local offices remain to be distributed as partisan rewards; gives examples (sergeants-at-arms, doorkeepers, clerks, postmasters, janitors, stenographers, election officers) and quantifies values (appointments within the President's gift estimated > $12,000,000 annually; New York legislature running expenses > $800,000; NYC pays > $400,000 for primary/election officials). Shows how appointment power at state and local levels supplies funds and patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levies on candidates and office-holders
rubrics_metrics.description: Party organizations...levy tribute from candidates for nominations as well as from nominees to office — generally in proportion to the value of the office they seek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes regular practice of assessing candidates (example testimony estimating $10,000–$25,000 for judicial nominations in NYC), and notes levies on office-holders after election despite prohibiting laws. Presents levies as a legitimate/expected contribution to campaign expenses and party machinery, with historical testimony (Mazet Commission).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public works and contracts as a source of party revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of parks, school buildings, highways, and other public works is a fruitful source of revenue to the party organization which controls the letting of contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how high bids may be accepted with the surplus diverted to party war chests or leaders; gives large-project examples (state capitol costs) and historical instances of 'plunder' during construction (e.g., Harrisburg capitol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate contributions and quid pro quo for franchises/permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions from corporations...have been the most fruitful source of revenue for party organizations within recent years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists affected industries (railway, insurance, banking, gas, electric, street railway, telegraph, express, telephone, public service corporations) and explains motivations (to secure franchises, permits, privileges). Describes corrupt practices: corporations find it cheaper to contribute to parties or be compelled to pay heavily to secure permits, with testimony (H.H. Vreeland, Metropolitan Street Railway) illustrating favors secured and impediments withdrawn after 'something had been done.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of vice (saloons, gambling) as a source of party revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The most despicable source of party revenue is that which is derived from the protection of saloons, gambling, and vice in a city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges difficulty of measuring extent, but cites evidence from cities (San Francisco, New York) showing party war chests augmented by money from criminal elements in exchange for police immunity. Flags this as particularly corrupt and morally objectionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized election administration by designated public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain officers — the secretary of state, county clerks, and in some instances special authorities — are placed in charge of the entire election process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (found in modern legislation) centralizes responsibility and oversight for the electoral process at administrative officers or authorities to ensure coherent administration across the jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bi-partisan boards of poll clerks and election inspectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions are made for bi-partisan boards of poll clerks, ballot clerks, and election inspectors in each polling place within the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation commonly requires representation from major parties among election officers at each polling place to reduce partisanship in administration and to increase confidence in the count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized party watchers at polling places
rubrics_metrics.description: Duly authorized watchers from each party may be present at each polling place in order to secure a fair count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits supervised observation by party-appointed watchers as a safeguard against fraud and to increase transparency of the in-person voting/counting process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard official tally sheets and certified returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard and official tally sheets, or records, on which to make the returns of each polling place, are furnished, and all returns must be certified by the proper officers in charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires uniform documentation for returns and official certification to ensure consistent aggregation and legal validity of election results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police at polling places and closure of saloons on election day
rubrics_metrics.description: Special arrangements are made to police polling places, and saloons are usually closed on election days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures to preserve order and reduce opportunities for intimidation or vote-buying near polling locations; closure of alcohol-serving establishments reduces inducements and corrupt practices tied to saloons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official registers of voters and pre-election voter registration/identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Official registers of voters are prepared before each election, and each citizen is entitled to enter his name so that on election day his right may be realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes strict registration schemes (example: New York 1908 law requiring personal identification, floor/room number, householder name, signature, and re-answering questions at the polls). Purpose: prevent false registration, detect 'floaters' and 'repeaters'; author notes salutary effects but acknowledges burdens and detailed procedures for illiterate voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot legislation to secure secrecy and encourage independent choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation on the ballot — designed to prevent intimidation by securing secrecy to the voter, and to encourage independent and discriminating choice from among the various candidates in place of the blind acceptance of party nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes secrecy (preventing intimidation/coercion), ballot design to enable voter independence, and broader reforms to counteract party domination of voting behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defects of 'vest-pocket' ballots (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vest-pocket ballot system left printing/distribution to parties and was deficient: chief among its defects was its utter failure to provide for secrecy in voting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists consequences/abuses: facilities for bribery (voter watched from receipt to deposit), coercion of economically dependent persons, printing expense deterring independent candidacies, distribution of misleading ballots (wrong candidates/emblems). Identifies why reform movement led to Australian ballot adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian ballot: public printing and official distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: All ballots used in elections of public officers...are printed under the direction of public officials, at public expense, and are distributed by these officials to the various polling places prior to the election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moves ballot production from parties to public authorities to prevent partisan printing abuses and reduce opportunities for manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian ballot: inclusion of all certified candidates and official endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each ballot contains on a single sheet the names of all the candidates duly nominated by any political party or independent group, whose names have been certified...and is protected against counterfeit by an official indorsement on the back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires inclusion of all certified candidates (party or independent), with official back endorsement as anti-counterfeit protection; candidates must be certified to officials a specified number of days before election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian ballot: in‑place acquisition and secret marking in voting booths
rubrics_metrics.description: Ballots are obtainable by the voters only within the polling places, on election day, from the regular election officials, and are to be marked in absolute secrecy in voting booths provided for the purpose, folded so as to conceal the marking on the face and yet leave exposed the official endorsement on the back, and returned to the election officers to be deposited in the ballot-box, before the voter leaves the polling place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes secrecy via in-place ballot receipt and private booths; folding conventions preserve endorsement visibility while concealing votes; return before leaving prevents outside tampering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian ballot: special safeguards for ballot security and accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Special safeguards...are usually provided to insure that the official ballots shall not be lost or stolen, or their contents divulged prior to election day; that none but official ballots shall be cast or counted; that the number of ballots counted shall correspond exactly with the number of persons voting, and that the ballot actually cast by each voter shall be the identical one given to him by the election officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists practical safeguards: systems (often detachable numbered stubs) to tie ballots to voter counts, prohibition of unauthorized ballots, prevention of electioneering in/around polling places, restricting access to specified persons, forbidding identifying marks, and prohibiting election officers or others from discovering/disclosing how any voter voted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Massachusetts (straight) ballot form characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Straight 'Massachusetts' ballot: names of the candidates of all parties are grouped in order (usually alphabetical) under the title of each office; only one method of marking — a cross opposite each candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Massachusetts (1888) also modified Australian model to recognize parties: defines political party based on vote percentage, allows party nomination certificates filed with the secretary, permits party designation to follow candidate name, and preserves alphabetical ordering; provides means (nomination papers) for independents and a right for voters to write names in blanks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indiana 'party column' ballot form and straight-ticket mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'party column' form groups all the candidates of each party in a separate column with the party name and device at the head and a 'party circle' by which the voter could vote a straight ticket with a single cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form (Indiana 1889) facilitates straight-ticket voting and, as noted, tends to discourage independent voting and preserve two-party dominance; empirical observations indicate party-column form has been the most popular historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified ballot forms (modified Massachusetts and modified Indiana)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variants: (a) modified 'Massachusetts' form preserves grouping by office but adds a provision for voting a straight party ticket; (b) modified 'Indiana' retains party-column grouping but requires marking each individual candidate (no straight-ticket device).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes compromises that blend candidate-grouping and straight-ticket features; gives earliest examples (Montana, Minnesota for modified Massachusetts; Missouri for modified Indiana) and their implications for independent voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot form effect on independent voting (empirical finding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the marking of each individual candidate on the ballot is compulsory the voters exercise from twice to ten times the discrimination among the candidates shown under the other ballot systems which favor straight voting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philip L. Allen's study (Political Science Quarterly, 1906) found that compulsory individual marking increases split-ticket/independent voting; states that favor straight-ticket mechanisms see lower rates of independent choice. Policy implication: ballot design materially affects voting behavior.
